content: 1. Alternative Providers for Injectable Contraceptives: For women in the post-abortion period who require contraception, the administration of injectable contraceptives by traditional and complementary medicine professionals, pharmacy workers, or community health workers is being evaluated as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to provision by trained health workers. Outcomes of interest include contraceptive uptake and continuation, safety (e.g., serious adverse events or complications), effectiveness (e.g., method failure), and user satisfaction. 2. Telemedicine for Medical Abortion: For pregnant individuals seeking medical abortion, telemedicine services—whether comprehensive or involving specific components such as eligibility assessment, counseling, facilitation of the procedure, or follow-up—are being assessed as a safe, effective, and satisfactory alternative to in-person care. Key outcomes include effectiveness (e.g., rates of ongoing pregnancy, success without surgical intervention), safety (e.g., adverse events or complications), satisfaction, adherence to recommended dosing regimens, and cost of services. 3. Community-Based Abortion Care: For pregnant individuals seeking induced abortion, community-based outreach models involving health workers are being considered as safe, effective, and acceptable alternatives to facility-based care provided by trained health workers. Outcomes include safety (e.g., adverse events or complications), effectiveness (e.g., success without surgical intervention), cost-effectiveness, increased health-seeking behaviors, and user satisfaction. These models are particularly relevant in settings with weak infrastructure or legal restrictions. 4. Harm-Reduction Counseling: For pregnant individuals seeking induced abortion, harm-reduction counseling on abortion care is being evaluated as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to routine in-clinic service delivery. Outcomes include safety (e.g., adverse events or complications), effectiveness (e.g., success without surgical intervention), and user satisfaction. This approach is applicable in both humanitarian and non-humanitarian settings. 5. Social Marketing for Safe Abortion Access: Social marketing outreach methods are being explored as a means to improve access to safe, effective, and acceptable abortion services compared to in-clinic care provided by trained health workers. Outcomes of interest include safety, effectiveness, access (e.g., affordability, utilization, attendance, and coverage), quality of care (e.g., method choice, information quality, provider competence), adverse effects (e.g., impact on existing services or inappropriate use), equitable access, cost, and user satisfaction. 6. Self-Sourcing Medications for Abortion: Pregnant individuals self-sourcing abortion medications through online platforms without a prescription are being evaluated as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to obtaining medications and prescriptions from trained health workers. Outcomes include safety (e.g., adverse events or complications), effectiveness (e.g., success without surgical intervention), medication quality, and user satisfaction. 7. Self-Administration of Injectable Contraceptives Post-Abortion: For individuals in the post-abortion period requiring contraception, self-administration of injectable contraceptives (for initiation or continuation) is being assessed as a safe, effective, and acceptable alternative to administration by trained health workers. Outcomes include contraceptive uptake and continuation, safety (e.g., adverse events or complications), effectiveness (e.g., method failure), and user satisfaction. 8. Guideline Dissemination and Updating: The WHO abortion care guideline will be disseminated digitally (interactive web-based and downloadable PDF formats) and in print. It will also be included in the annually updated compendium of WHO-approved recommendations. Dissemination will occur through NGO partners, professional associations, and social media platforms. Translations into Spanish, French, Portuguese, and other languages will be developed as needed. The guideline will be launched through regional dissemination meetings, with adaptation and implementation research conducted in select countries. Supporting materials, such as PowerPoint presentations and social media content, will aid in spreading key messages. 9. Living Guideline Approach: The guideline will be presented online in an interactive format, allowing it to function as a living guideline. This approach facilitates continuous review of new research evidence, enabling timely updates to recommendations. The guideline consolidates and updates recommendations from three previous WHO guidelines on abortion care. 10. Archiving and Evidence Review: All technical products developed during the guideline process, including systematic review reports and search strategies, will be archived for future reference. If new evidence raises concerns about the validity of a recommendation, the systematic review will be updated using the original search strategy. New questions identified will undergo a similar evidence retrieval and synthesis process, adhering to WHO standards for guideline development. This content reflects a comprehensive and evidence-based approach to improving abortion care and post-abortion contraception, with a focus on safety, effectiveness, accessibility, and user satisfaction.
